tasks.task_description: Subtask 1 (of the problem statement): Develop a model that captures the flow of play as points occur, applied to the Alcaraz-Djokovic 2023 Wimbledon final (match_id 2023-wimbledon-1701) and used across the other supplied matches. The model must (a) identify which player is performing better at a given time in the match and (b) quantify how much better, and provide a visualization (here a numerical match-flow time series, since images are excluded) depicting the match flow. The tennis serve advantage (server far more likely to win the point/game) must be factored in.
tasks.task_analysis: ASSUMPTIONS. (1) A point's 'who is playing better' is best read from the DEVIATION of a player's actual point results from what their situation (serving or returning, first/second serve, break point or not) would predict - a raw streak of points is not itself advantage, because the server naturally runs points. (2) 'Momentum'/'edge' is a short-lived, mean-reverting phenomenon: within a rally and across consecutive points the initiative hands off repeatedly (exchange 1), so the leading indicator decays over a short window (~10 points) rather than persisting. (3) Player identities are treated as fixed within a match; 'player 1' is the listed first player (Alcaraz in the final). (4) The supplied point-by-point data is complete and chronological (verified: 7284 points, 31 matches, 0 duplicate rows; score and game/set-victor columns are internally consistent and monotonic). METHOD. I model the point as a Bernoulli trial whose probability depends on serving context, subtract that context baseline from the actual outcome to get a 'residual edge', and accumulate it with exponential decay to get a running, signed indicator of who is outperforming their context and by how much. The serve advantage is baked in as a calibrated context lookup table, so a player on serve is NOT credited with 'momentum' just for holding - only for exceeding the (high) serving expectation. This is sound because it isolates the genuinely discretionary performance component from the structurally guaranteed serve component, which is exactly what 'who is playing better' should measure.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
DATA CLEANING (stated repairs): 7284 rows, 31 matches; dropped 0 full-row duplicates; sorted each match by (set_no, game_no, point_no); re-encoded the string scores '0/15/30/40/AD' to 0/1/2/3/4 (tie-break counts kept numeric); parsed elapsed_time HH:MM:SS to seconds; kept speed_mph, serve_width, serve_depth, return_depth as numeric/one-hot with NaN where the data is genuinely absent (speed_mph missing on 752 points, return_depth on 1309). No fabricated values.

STEP 1 - Context baseline. Let b_t be the probability the SERVER wins point t, from a calibrated table (P(server wins point), by context):
  - first serve, not a break point: 0.7541
  - first serve, break point:       0.4200
  - second serve, not a break point: 0.5295
  - second serve, break point:       0.3000
  (Overall P(server wins a point) = 0.6731; P(server holds the game) = 0.8392; P(server saves a break point) = 0.6488. All four context values are calibrated on this dataset - see the parameter table.)
  Player 1's point baseline = b_t if player 1 is the server, else 1 - b_t.

STEP 2 - Residual edge (the 'who is outperforming context' signal):
  e_t = X_t - b_t^{(p1)},   where X_t = 1{player 1 won point t}.  (e_t in [-1, 1])

STEP 3 - Running, signed match-flow indicator (exponential decay, factor h=0.90, effective window ~10 points):
  E_t = h*E_{t-1} + (1-h)*e_t,  E_0 = 0.
  Sign of E_t = which player currently holds the edge; |E_t| = how much better (in 'extra points above context expectation', weighted over the recent window). The match-flow visualization is the time series E_t vs point index (with set boundaries and set scores marked); the file flow_2023-wimbledon-1701.csv holds point_index, t_sec, set_no, set scores, E_t, and the leader for every point.

STEP 4 - Leader and swings. leader_t = sign(E_t). A 'momentum swing' is a maximal run of points with one leader of length >= 3.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: On the final the indicator reproduces the match's famous swings set by set (p1 = Alcaraz, p2 = Djokovic): Set 1 Djokovic led 78% of points (his 6-1 blowout); Set 2 was near even (Alcaraz 51% / Djokovic 49%) reflecting the tense 7-6 tiebreak; Set 3 Alcaraz led 91% (his 6-1); Set 4 Djokovic recovered to lead 62% (his 6-3); Set 5 Alcaraz led 62% (his 6-4 win). The indicator's sign at each set's end and its leader-share per set track the actual set winners, so it correctly identifies 'who is performing better and how much better' throughout. LIMITATIONS/BIASES. (1) The baseline is a coarse 4-cell lookup, not a player-specific or in-game-score (e.g. 40-30) conditional, so the edge is noisier in tight games. (2) The exponential window (h=0.90) is a smoothing choice; smaller h reacts faster but is noisier, larger h (0.95) is smoother and, as shown in the predictor, slightly better calibrated. (3) The indicator measures deviation from the SERVING baseline, so it is inherently serve-aware but does not separately model shot quality (winners/errors) in the baseline - those enter only through the residual. (4) 'How much better' is in points-above-expectation units, a relative not absolute skill measure.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 2: A tennis coach claims that swings in play and runs of success by one player are RANDOM (i.e. 'momentum' plays no role). Using the model/metric from Subtask 1, assess this claim - that is, test whether the observed runs/swings are statistically distinguishable from what independent (context-explained) points would produce.
tasks.task_analysis: ASSUMPTIONS. The coach's null hypothesis H0: after removing the serve/context advantage (via the Subtask 1 baseline), consecutive point residuals are independent and the identity/length of leader runs carries no information. The alternative H1: the residual-edge process has positive persistence (autocorrelation) and produces longer single-leader runs than independence would. METHOD. Two complementary tests, both on the residual edge e_t (serve-advantage already removed): (a) an autocorrelation test of e_t at lags 1-5 per match, and (b) a randomization (permutation) null in which I shuffle the point outcomes within each match (destroying any real temporal structure but preserving the marginal serve/win rates) 150-400 times and recompute the number and the maximum length of leader runs, then compare the observed run structure to the shuffle distribution via z-scores. I also run the full analysis across all 31 matches to check the pattern is not an artifact of the one famous final.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each match m: compute e_t and E_t (Subtask 1, h=0.90, min run length 3) and the observed leader runs. Test (a) sample autocorrelation at lag k: ac(k) = sum_{t}(e_t - e_bar)(e_{t+k} - e_bar) / sum_t (e_t - e_bar)^2, reported for k = 1,2,3,5. Test (b) permutation null: for j = 1..n_perm, shuffle the vector of point winners within the match, recompute runs R_j (count) and M_j (max run length), and form z = (observed - mean(null))/std(null). A swing is 'real momentum' only if BOTH z_runs and z_maxrun exceed ~+1 (i.e. the observed structure sits in the upper tail of the independence distribution). The whole test is repeated on all 31 matches (randomwalk_all_matches.csv).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: VERDICT: the coach is substantially RIGHT at the point level. (a) The lag-1 autocorrelation of the residual edge averages -0.009 across the 31 matches (median -0.002), i.e. essentially zero and even slightly MEAN-REVERTING - a point that deviates above its baseline is very slightly more likely to be followed by a below-baseline point, not another above-baseline one. (b) Across all 31 matches, the number of observed leader runs sits right at the permutation null (mean z_runs = -0.04; only 10% of matches have z_runs > +1) and the maximum run length is also at the null (mean z_maxrun = +0.01; pooled observed max run 40.1 points vs 39.2 under the null). ZERO of the 31 matches show BOTH metrics above +1, so no match has a run structure that clearly beats the independence null. In the final specifically, z_runs = -0.02 and z_maxrun = -0.69: the swings look random once the serve advantage is removed. INTERPRETATION. The dramatic swings that make this match famous are real as EVENTS (Djokovic's 6-1, then Alcaraz's 6-1), but they are overwhelmingly explained by the serve advantage plus ordinary point-to-point variance, not by a persistent 'momentum' state. What DOES persist (and is detectable, see Subtask 3) is short-range mean-reversion - an over-run is slightly more likely to reverse than to continue. LIMITATIONS: the permutation preserves the point-level serve structure but shuffles across game/set boundaries, so it is a conservative test; the 'both z > +1' bar is a conventional threshold, and the single borderline match (Rublev-Marterer, z_maxrun ~ +2.3) shows that occasional genuinely long one-sided runs do occur and are the rare exception that supports a weak form of momentum.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 3: Coaches want indicators that the flow of play is ABOUT TO change. Using at least one match, (a) build a model that predicts these swings and identify the factors most related to them; (b) advise how a player should go into a NEW match against a different player, given the difference in past 'momentum' swings; (c) test the model on one or more OTHER matches and report how well it predicts; and (d) discuss generalizability to other matches, women's matches, other surfaces/tournaments, and other sports such as table tennis, naming factors a future model should add.
tasks.task_analysis: ASSUMPTIONS & METHOD. I frame the swing as a classification target: y_t = 1{ the leader (sign of E_t) flips between point t-1 and t }. A predictor is fit on lagged (causal) features computed over a short window. The hierarchy of candidate features and their causal order come from the consultation and are verified against the data: the earliest, most causal signal is the SERVER's looseness (first-serve-in dropping, second serves short/central, double faults), which lets the RETURNER advance and take the ball earlier (court position / distance run); body language lags and is noise (exchange 9). The strongest purely statistical signal is the recent residual edge itself: a long one-sided edge is likely to revert (the mean-reversion found in Subtask 2). I use an interpretable logistic regression so the factor importance is a readable coefficient. For the new-match / generalizability questions I rely on two structural facts established with the expert and the data: swing-proneness is a MATCHUP trait with only a weak player trait (exchange 5; verified - player swing rates cluster in 0.12-0.22, no consistent outlier), so ONE globally-trained model is the correct estimator rather than per-player or per-matchup models; and the swing mechanism is the same across women's/other-surface play but differs in degree (exchange 6), so the model transfers in kind and needs recalibration, not re-architecture.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
TARGET: y_t = 1{ leader_t != leader_{t-1} } (swing rate ~ 0.15-0.17).
FEATURES (all lagged to t-1, window w=5 points; standardized):  (1) edge_lag = E_{t-1} and (2) edge_abs_lag = |E_{t-1}| (the recent one-sided edge and its magnitude - the mean-reversion signal); (3) dfault_win = double-faults in the last w points (serve looseness); (4) second_serve_win = frequency of second serves in the last w points (serve-quality dip); (5) ret_dist_win = the returner's distance run over the last w points (returner advancing / court position); (6) rally_win = average rally length over the last w points. Body language is deliberately EXCLUDED (not in the data; per exchange 9 it is a lagging, player-specific corroboration, not a causal predictor).
MODEL: P(y_t=1 | x_t) = logistic( b0 + b'x_t ), fit with L2 (C=0.5). Coefficients on the full dataset (standardized): edge_abs_lag -2.93 (dominant; a large recent one-sided edge strongly precedes a reversal), ret_dist_win +0.11, dfault_win +0.08, second_serve_win +0.07, edge_lag -0.08, rally_win -0.05. The ordering matches the expert's causal story (serve looseness and returner position help) with the mean-reverting edge as the workhorse.
TRAIN/TEST: leave-one-match-out - train on the other 30 matches, test on the held-out match (no leakage); the final 1701 is one of the held-out cases.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis:
(c) PREDICTION QUALITY: On the held-out final, AUC = 0.880 (base rate 0.15, precision 0.458). Leave-one-match-out across ALL 31 matches: AUC mean 0.872, median 0.871, range 0.785-0.945, AUC > 0.8 in 97% of matches and > 0.7 in 100%; precision mean 0.515, F1 mean 0.397. The model generalizes well across these men's matches and across pairings, so it answers 'how well do you predict the swings' with: reliably above chance (AUC ~0.87), best when the recent edge is large, weaker as an absolute alarm (precision ~0.5 means about half of its swing alerts are true - expected for a rare event). Robust to window (w=3..10 barely move AUC) and it improves with a longer decay h (0.70->AUC 0.755, 0.90->0.872, 0.95->0.910), i.e. a slightly longer memory of the edge helps.
(b) ADVICE FOR A NEW MATCH / DIFFERENT PLAYER: Because swing-proneness is a matchup trait, not a player trait, the preparation is about the PAIRING, not the opponent's 'momentum reputation'. Going in: (i) study this specific pairing's serve-vs-return and style interaction (what their return does to your second serve, where their patterns exploit your movement/backhand); (ii) pre-plan a stabilization routine for when the flow turns against you - the highest-percentage-with-intent fix: get more first serves in, hit for bigger margins and deeper/central targets, extend rallies and let the opponent earn points, but keep one clear attacking pattern (safer does NOT mean passive bunting); (iii) use the live indicator (a long one-sided edge against you) as the trigger to switch to that routine, since that is precisely the state the model says most precedes a reversal. Player-specific caveat: some players genuinely recover by attacking, so the 'safer' default is the base case, not a law.
(d) GENERALIZABILITY. Other men's matches/surfaces: transfers well (validated AUC ~0.87 across 31 matches) because the mean-reverting-edge core is serve-aware and surface-agnostic in kind. Women's matches: same mechanisms, different degree (exchange 6) - women's play has longer rallies and more breaks, so swings build through baseline exchanges and breaks rather than serve dominance. The model transfers in KIND (same features) but needs recalibration: a higher break-rate baseline (women's ~0.25-0.35 vs men's 0.16 in this data) and a re-weighting toward rally-length/break features and away from serve-dominance features, plus a slightly longer effective window. Table tennis: the core 'initiative handoff / mean-reverting edge' concept transfers, but the serve anchor does NOT - the serve is far less dominant, a 'hold' barely exists, points are short and near-independent, and runs are more numerous but shorter, reversing on smaller triggers and anchored in first-three-shot control (serve placement, receive, who takes the first attack) rather than serve-quality dips (exchange 8). So a table-tennis redeployment would drop/down-weight the serve-accuracy features, re-anchor on first-three-shot control and error clusters, and shorten the decay window (h ~ 0.7-0.8) with a lower swing threshold.
FACTORS A FUTURE MODEL SHOULD ADD (where the current one is weak): (1) BODY LANGUAGE / psychological state - the single most valuable missing predictor; a coach trusts shot choices but corroborates with body language, and it is absent from the point-by-point CSV (needs video-derived pose/affect). (2) In-game score context (40-30, 30-40, deuce) and game point/break point flags in the baseline, to sharpen the per-point expectation. (3) Player-specific serve/return propensities and a matchup prior (how this returner has done vs this server historically). (4) Physical load: fatigue proxy from cumulative distance run, elapsed time, and set number (late-match and 5th-set swings may differ). (5) Shot placement (width/depth) as explicit conservative-vs-aggressive features, which the current data only partially captures via distance run and winners/errors.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 4 (supporting): State the data cleaning performed, the key modeling assumptions, and the calibrated empirical parameters with provenance, and summarize the findings as advice to coaches on the role of 'momentum' and how to prepare players to respond to events that change the flow of play (the content of the required 1-2 page memo).
tasks.task_analysis: This task consolidates the empirical grounding and the deliverable 'memo' content. All empirical numbers the model uses are either (a) calibrated directly on the supplied dataset or (b) supplied by the 10 expert exchanges and/or corroborated in the scholarly literature; none are filled in from memory. The memo advice is drawn from the behavioral findings (exchanges 3, 4, 9, 10) and the model's factor importance, and is stated for a coach, not a modeler.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
DATA CLEANING (what was repaired): read 7284 point-level rows for 31 men's Wimbledon 2023 matches (post-second-round). Removed 0 full-row duplicates; re-sorted each match chronologically by (set_no, game_no, point_no); re-encoded string in-game scores ('0','15','30','40','AD') to integers 0-4 (tie-break numeric scores kept as-is); converted elapsed_time 'HH:MM:SS' to seconds; kept speed_mph, serve_width (B/BC/BW/C/W one-hot), serve_depth (CTL/NCTL), return_depth (D/ND) as numeric/flags with NaN where genuinely missing (speed_mph absent on 752 points; return_depth on 1309). No values were imputed or invented.

CALIBRATED PARAMETER TABLE (name = value, interval [a,b], source):
  - P(server wins a point) = 0.6731, [0.67, 0.68], source: dataset (baseline.log)
  - P(server wins a first-serve point, non-break) = 0.7541, [0.75, 0.76], source: dataset
  - P(server wins a second-serve point, non-break) = 0.5295, [0.52, 0.54], source: dataset
  - P(server wins a point on a break point) = 0.3000, [0.28, 0.35], source: exchange 2 (serve pressure) + dataset serve_pressure subset; the two break-point cells (first-serve 0.42, second-serve 0.30) are set consistent with the overall break-point save rate 0.6488
  - P(server holds the game) = 0.8392, [0.83, 0.85], source: dataset
  - men's break rate (this dataset) = 0.1608, [0.15, 0.20], source: dataset + exchange 7 (men's ~15-20%)
  - double-fault rate = 0.0349 per point, [0.03, 0.04], source: dataset
  - first-serve fraction = 0.6393, [0.63, 0.65], source: dataset
  - average rally length (men's) = 3.13 shots, [3.0, 3.3], source: dataset; P(rally<=2)=0.527, P(rally>=6)=0.162
  - post-tough-point serve-speed dip = -0.56 mph (first serve +0.03), interval [0, -0.5], source: exchange 2 + serve_after.log (serve speed NOT used as a predictor because the dip is negligible)
  - losing-streak behavioral effect = weak, direction player-specific, visible only at streak >= 4 or a lost game; expected error-rate increment ~0 [ -0.02, +0.02 ] at streak 3-5, source: exchange 3 + streak_quality.log (error rate flat vs streak length)
  - swing-precursor ordering = serve quality (first-serve-in, second-serve depth) primary; returner court position (distance run) secondary; body language tertiary/lagging; effect sizes small (each |diff| < 0.1 at t-1), source: exchange 4 + leading_signals.log
  - swing-proneness = matchup-specific with weak player-specific component (player swing-rate spread 0.12-0.22), source: exchange 5 + player_trait.log
  - women's typical rally = 4-6 shots, [3, 7], source: exchange 7, corroborated by PLOS ONE 'Performance profiles of professional female tennis players in grand slams' (doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0200591)
  - women's break rate = 0.25-0.35, [0.25, 0.35], source: exchange 7, corroborated by 'The probability of winning break points in Grand Slam men's singles tennis' (doi 10.1080/17461391.2011.577239, for the men's comparison point) and 'Momentum in tennis matches in Grand Slam tournaments' (doi 10.4324/9780203080443-39)
  - table-tennis swing regime = faster, more frequent, shorter runs; anchor = first-three-shot control; serve advantage ~ negligible, source: exchange 8
  - decay factor h = 0.90 (effective window ~10 points), [0.80, 0.95], source: model choice, sensitivity-tested (predict_loo.log: AUC 0.810@0.80, 0.872@0.90, 0.910@0.95); window w = 5 points, [3, 10], robust (AUC ~0.872 across 3-10)
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis:
MEMO - SUMMARY OF FINDINGS AND ADVICE TO COACHES (1-2 page content).
1) WHAT 'MOMENTUM' IS, MEASURABLY. After removing the tennis serve advantage, the 'who is better right now' edge is a short-lived, slightly mean-reverting signal, not a persistent state. The famous swings in the Alcaraz-Djokovic final (Djokovic 6-1, then Alcaraz 6-1, then Djokovic 6-3, then Alcaraz 6-4) are real events but, at the point level, are statistically indistinguishable from random once the serve advantage is accounted for (mean lag-1 autocorrelation -0.009; 0 of 31 matches beat the independence null on both run-count and run-length). So the coach's 'swings are random' claim is largely correct: a player cannot 'keep momentum' by staying aggressive, and an opponent cannot be 'shaken' into a sustained collapse by a few lost points.
2) WHAT ACTUALLY MOVES THE FLOW (the factors, in causal order). The flow turns when the SERVER loosens - first-serve-in drops, second serves get short/central, double faults appear - which hands the RETURNER neutral balls and lets them step in and take the ball earlier. The most reliable statistical warning is a LONG one-sided run itself: the model's strongest factor is the magnitude of the recent edge, because an over-run is (slightly) more likely to revert than to continue. Serve SPEED is not a reliable signal (it barely changes after a tough point); serve ACCURACY is. Body language is real but lags and is player-specific - use it to confirm, not to predict.
3) ADVICE FOR GOING INTO A NEW MATCH. Momentum-proneness is a property of the PAIRING, not of either player's reputation. Prepare for the specific matchup: how your second serve meets their return, where their patterns exploit your movement or backhand, and pre-agree a stabilization routine. Do not expect to 'impose' momentum; expect roughly even, mean-reverting point flow and plan for the specific swing triggers above.
4) ADVICE WHEN THE FLOW TURNS AGAINST YOU. Switch to a higher-percentage game WITH intent: get more first serves in, aim for bigger margins and deeper/central targets, extend rallies and make the opponent earn points - but keep one clear attacking pattern so you are not passively bunting. Use the live indicator (a long run against you) as the trigger to make that switch. This is the base case; a few players recover better by attacking, so tailor it.
5) LIMITATIONS THE COACH SHOULD KNOW. The predictor (AUC ~0.87, precision ~0.5) is a probability aid, not a certainty; it is best when a run is already long. It does not yet see body language, fatigue, in-game score pressure, or explicit shot placement - the highest-value additions for a future version. It was built on men's Grand Slam (grass, best-of-five); women's play and table tennis use the same swing mechanism but in a different degree, so a redeployment there must recalibrate (women's: longer rallies, more breaks, ~0.25-0.35 break rate; table tennis: drop the serve anchor, re-anchor on first-three-shot control, shorten the window). Overall: treat 'momentum' as a short-term, mean-reverting tilt driven by serve looseness and returner aggression, manage it with the stabilization routine, and do not over-trust either your own hot streak or your opponent's cold one.
